We have mass spec peak at m/z 224.12 (M+? likely molecular ion). No charge indicated, likely M+? So molecular weight ~224.12. Carbon NMR shows many aromatic carbons: many around 128-129, plus 196.8 (likely carbonyl C=O), 143,139,135,127 etc. Also aliphatic carbons: 37.5, 36.39, 26.41. So likely aromatic ring with carbonyl (maybe benzophenone derivative). Molecular weight 224 suggests C? Let's guess formula. Use typical aromatic C6H5 = 77. So two phenyl rings = 154. Add carbonyl C=O adds 28 (C=12 O=16) = 182. Need extra 42 mass. Could be a tert-butyl? tBu = C4H9 = 57. Too high. Maybe a methyl (15) plus something else. Let's compute possible formula: C15H12O? C15=180, H12=12, O=16 total 208. Not 224. C16H12O? 192+12+16=220. C16H14O? 192+14+16=222. C16H16O? 192+16+16=224. So C16H16O fits mass 224. That's likely. C16H16O has DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 =16 -8 +1 =9. So 9 degrees unsaturation. Aromatic rings give 4 each (two rings =8) plus carbonyl double bond =1 =>9 fits. So structure likely a benzophenone with two phenyl rings and a carbonyl, plus maybe extra substituents to give H16. Benzophenone (diphenyl ketone) formula C13H10O? Actually benzophenone is C13H10O? Wait benzophenone: C6H5-CO-C6H5 = C13H10O (C13=156, H10=10, O=16 total 182). So need extra C3H6 (42) to reach 224. Could be a propyl group on one phenyl. So maybe 4'-propylbenzophenone? That would be C16H16O indeed (C13 + C3 = C16, H10+H6=H16). So structure: phenyl-CO-phenyl with propyl substituent on one ring. NMR: aromatic carbons many signals (maybe substituted ring reduces symmetry). Aliphatic carbons: 37.5, 36.39, 26.41 correspond to propyl chain (CH2-CH2-CH3). Chemical shifts: CH2 attached to aromatic ~ 37, next CH2 ~ 26, CH3 ~ 14 but we have 36.39 maybe CH attached to carbonyl? Actually carbonyl carbon is 196.8. So aliphatic: 37.5 (CH2 attached to aromatic), 36.39 maybe CH2 attached to carbonyl? Wait carbonyl attached to aromatic, not to propyl. Propyl attached to aromatic: CH2 (benzylic) ~ 37, CH2 ~ 26, CH3 ~ 14 but we have 26.41 and 36.39 maybe two CH2, missing CH3? Could be isopropyl? Isopropyl gives two CH3 ~ 22, CH ~ 30. Not match. Maybe a tert-butyl: quaternary carbon ~ 40, methyls ~ 30. Not.

But we have only three aliphatic carbons: 37.5, 36.39, 26.41. Could be a cyclohexyl? But then more signals.

Maybe it's a phenylacetophenone: phenyl-CO-CH2-Ph? That would be C15H12O? Actually phenylacetophenone: C6H5-CO-CH2-C6H5 = C15H12O (MW 212). Not.

Our formula C16H16O suggests maybe a benzophenone with a methyl on one ring and an ethyl on other? But aliphatic carbons count 3 distinct: maybe ethyl (CH2 36, CH3 26) plus methyl attached to carbonyl? No.

Check carbonyl carbon 196.8 typical for ketone. Aromatic carbons many duplicates: we have pairs: 129.50 (x2), 129.01 (x2), 128.90 (x2), 128.50 (x2) suggests two phenyl rings with similar but not identical substitution. Additional aromatic carbons: 143.10, 139.03, 135.88, 127.20. Those likely ipso and substituted positions.

Thus likely a mono-substituted benzophenone with a propyl group (C3) on one ring. Propyl gives CH2 (benzylic) ~ 37, CH2 ~ 26, CH3 ~ 14 but we don't see 14. Maybe the CH3 is overlapped with aromatic? Not.

But maybe the aliphatic carbon at 36.39 is the carbonyl carbon? No carbonyl is 196.8. So 36.39 could be CH2 attached to carbonyl (alpha carbon) if we have a phenyl-CO-CH2-CH3 (acetophenone with ethyl). That would be C15H14O? Actually ethyl phenyl ketone: C6H5-CO-CH2-CH3 = C9? Wait count: phenyl (C6H5) + CO (C1O1) + CH2CH3 (C2H5) = C9? No total C6+1+2=9? That's wrong. Let's compute: phenyl = C6H5, carbonyl carbon = C1, ethyl = C2H5 => total C9? Actually C6+1+2 =9, H5+5=10, O1 => C9H10O? That's 138. Not.

Our molecule has two phenyl rings, so benzophenone core plus extra alkyl.

Thus propose SMILES: CC(C)C(=O)C1=CC=CC=C1C2=CC=CC=C2? That's t-butyl? That would be C16H16O? t-butyl attached to carbonyl (pivalophenone). That gives carbonyl attached to t-butyl and phenyl. But we need two phenyl rings? Actually pivalophenone is phenyl-CO-C(CH3)3, formula C11? Wait phenyl (C6H5) + CO (C1O) + C(CH3)3 (C4H9) = C11? Actually C6+1+4=11, H5+9=14, O1 => C11H14O = 162. Not.

Our mass 224 suggests two phenyl rings plus propyl.

SMILES: CCCc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)c2ccccc2 . That's propyl attached to phenyl ring (para maybe). That is C16H16O. Let's verify: phenyl (C6H5) + carbonyl carbon (C1) + second phenyl (C6H5) = C13H10O. Add propyl C3H7 = C16H17O? Wait adding propyl replaces a hydrogen on phenyl, so net add C3H7 - H = C3H6. So C13H10O + C3H6 = C16H16O. Yes.

Thus SMILES: CCCc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)c2ccccc2 . Need aromatic ring with propyl substituent. Could be "CCCc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)c2ccccc2". That seems plausible.

Check aliphatic carbons: CH2 attached to aromatic (benzylic) ~ 37, CH2 next ~ 26, CH3 ~ 14 (not observed). Maybe CH3 shift overlapped with aromatic? But 14 not present. However maybe the CH3 is at 26.41? No.

But we have only three aliphatic signals, could be CH3 not resolved. Could be that CH3 shift is 26.41 (unlikely). But maybe the chain is isopropyl: CH (attached to aromatic) ~ 37, two CH3 ~ 22 each. We have 36.39 and 26.41 maybe CH and CH3? Not.

Nevertheless likely answer.

We could also validate formula via get_formula_from_smiles.
